title: Radioactivity & Nuclear Physics
description: Types of radiation, half-life, nuclear decay equations, uses and dangers of radiation, fission and fusion.

notes.heading: What is Radioactivity?
notes.body: Radioactivity is the spontaneous decay of unstable atomic nuclei, emitting radiation. Discovered by Henri Becquerel (1896); studied by Marie and Pierre Curie. An unstable nucleus has too many or too few neutrons relative to protons. Decay is RANDOM — you cannot predict when an individual nucleus will decay, but you can predict the behaviour of large numbers (half-life). Decay is unaffected by temperature, pressure, or chemical bonding — it is a nuclear process, not chemical. Radiation can be: particulate (alpha, beta) or electromagnetic (gamma). All three types are IONISING — they can knock electrons off atoms, creating ions. This makes them dangerous (can damage DNA → cancer) but also useful (sterilisation, cancer treatment).

illustration.alt: Unstable nucleus emitting alpha, beta, and gamma radiation, with key facts about radioactivity.
illustration.caption: Radioactive decay is a random nuclear process discovered by Henri Becquerel in 1896.

notes.heading: Alpha, Beta and Gamma Radiation
notes.body: Alpha (α): helium nucleus — 2 protons + 2 neutrons. Mass 4, charge +2. Penetration: stopped by paper or a few cm of air. Ionisation: VERY high (strongly ionising). Deflected by electric/magnetic fields (positive charge). Used in smoke detectors (americium-241). Beta (β): fast-moving electron emitted when a neutron turns into a proton (n → p + e⁻ + antineutrino). Mass ~0, charge −1. Penetration: stopped by ~3 mm aluminium. Ionisation: moderate. Deflected opposite to alpha in fields. Used for thickness monitoring in paper/aluminium production. Gamma (γ): electromagnetic wave (not a particle). No mass, no charge. Penetration: highly penetrating — reduced by thick lead or concrete (never completely stopped). Ionisation: weak. Not deflected by fields. Used for sterilising medical equipment, cancer radiotherapy. Neutron radiation: emitted during fission; very penetrating (stopped by thick concrete/water).

illustration.alt: Penetration comparison showing paper stops alpha, aluminium stops beta, and lead is needed for gamma.
illustration.caption: Alpha is the most ionising but least penetrating; gamma is the least ionising but most penetrating.

notes.heading: Nuclear Decay Equations
notes.body: In nuclear equations, the total mass number (top) and atomic number (bottom) must balance. Alpha decay: mass decreases by 4, atomic number by 2. ²³⁸₉₂U → ²³⁴₉₀Th + ⁴₂He (α). The element changes — transmutation. Beta decay: mass unchanged, atomic number increases by 1 (neutron → proton). ¹⁴₆C → ¹⁴₇N + ⁰₋₁e (β). Gamma emission: no change to mass or atomic number — just energy release. ⁶⁰₂₈Ni* → ⁶⁰₂₈Ni + γ. Often accompanies alpha/beta decay when the daughter nucleus is in an excited state. Positron emission (β⁺): proton → neutron + positron + neutrino. Atomic number decreases by 1. Used in PET scans. Electron capture: nucleus captures an inner electron, proton becomes neutron. Atomic number decreases by 1.

illustration.alt: Alpha and beta decay equations showing how mass and atomic numbers change during radioactive decay.
illustration.caption: In alpha decay the nucleus loses 2 protons and 2 neutrons; in beta decay a neutron turns into a proton.

notes.heading: Half-Life
notes.body: Half-life (t½) is the time taken for half the radioactive nuclei in a sample to decay. It is constant for a given isotope, unaffected by physical conditions. After 1 half-life: ½ remains. After 2: ¼. After 3: ⅛. After n half-lives: (½)ⁿ remains. Calculating from a graph: find time when activity/count rate drops by half. Carbon-14 dating: t½ = 5730 years. Living organisms have constant ¹⁴C ratio (from CO₂ in atmosphere). After death, ¹⁴C decays without replenishment. Measuring remaining ¹⁴C gives the time since death (up to ~50,000 years). Uses of half-life: medical tracers (short t½ — technetium-99m, t½=6 h, gamma emitter → detected outside body), dating rocks (uranium-lead, t½ ~4.5 billion years), monitoring radioactive waste storage duration.

illustration.alt: Radioactive decay curve showing exponential decrease with half-life markers at each halving.
illustration.caption: Half-life is the time taken for half the radioactive nuclei in a sample to decay.

notes.heading: Uses and Dangers of Radiation
notes.body: Uses: (1) Medicine — radiotherapy (gamma rays target and kill cancer cells), diagnostic tracers (gamma emitters with short t½ injected and tracked — PET, SPECT scans), sterilising surgical equipment (gamma). (2) Industry — thickness monitoring (beta particles — if fewer detected, material is too thick), detecting leaks in underground pipes (tracer), smoke alarms (alpha). (3) Food — gamma irradiation kills bacteria/pests, extends shelf life. (4) Archaeology/geology — carbon-14 dating (organic material), uranium-lead dating (rocks). Dangers: ionising radiation damages DNA molecules → mutations → cancer. High doses: radiation sickness, burns, organ failure, death. Alpha is most dangerous INSIDE the body (if inhaled/ingested — strongly ionises nearby cells). Outside body: alpha stopped by dead skin layer; beta and gamma penetrate → dangerous from external sources. Safety: minimise exposure TIME, maximise DISTANCE (inverse square law — double distance = quarter dose), use SHIELDING (lead for gamma, aluminium for beta, paper for alpha).

illustration.alt: Medical uses of radiation (tracers, radiotherapy, sterilisation) and the difference between contamination and irradiation.
illustration.caption: Radiation has many beneficial uses in medicine but must be handled with care to avoid harm.

notes.heading: Nuclear Fission
notes.body: Fission: a large, unstable nucleus (e.g., uranium-235, plutonium-239) absorbs a neutron and splits into two smaller nuclei (daughter products), releasing 2-3 neutrons + enormous energy (E=mc² — mass converted to energy). The neutrons can trigger further fissions → CHAIN REACTION. If controlled: nuclear power station (heat → steam → turbine → electricity). If uncontrolled: atomic bomb. Control rods (boron/cadmium) absorb excess neutrons, keeping the chain reaction steady. Moderator (water/graphite) slows neutrons to increase probability of causing fission. Fission products are radioactive waste — dangerous for thousands of years, requiring secure storage. The energy released is ~200 MeV per fission — millions of times more than chemical reactions per atom. Nuclear power: no CO₂ emissions during operation, very high energy density, but radioactive waste and accident risks (Chernobyl 1986, Fukushima 2011).

illustration.alt: Uranium-235 fission chain reaction diagram showing neutron absorption, splitting, and more neutrons released.
illustration.caption: Nuclear fission splits a large nucleus, releasing energy and neutrons that can trigger a chain reaction.

notes.heading: Nuclear Fusion
notes.body: Fusion: two light nuclei combine to form a heavier nucleus, releasing energy. This powers the Sun and other stars. Example: deuterium (²H) + tritium (³H) → ⁴He + n + energy. Fusion requires EXTREME temperature and pressure to overcome electrostatic repulsion between positively charged nuclei (the Coulomb barrier). In stars, gravity provides this. On Earth, magnetic confinement (tokamaks — ITER project) or inertial confinement (lasers) attempts to achieve fusion. Advantages over fission: fuel abundant (deuterium from seawater), no long-lived radioactive waste (main product is helium — inert), no risk of meltdown (reaction self-limits if conditions fail), much higher energy output per mass. Challenge: currently requires more energy input to sustain than it produces (though JET and NIF have achieved brief net energy gain). Fusion is the 'holy grail' of energy — clean, safe, virtually unlimited. Cold fusion: controversial claims not replicated — not accepted by mainstream science.

illustration.alt: Hydrogen isotopes fusing to form helium, releasing enormous energy — the process powering the Sun.
illustration.caption: Nuclear fusion joins small nuclei together and releases even more energy than fission per unit mass.

flashcards.definition: Spontaneous decay of unstable nuclei, emitting ionising radiation. Random process — cannot predict individual decays.
flashcards.example: Uranium decays over billions of years; technetium-99m has half-life of 6 hours.

flashcards.definition: Helium nucleus (2p+2n). Highly ionising. Stopped by paper/skin. Deflected by fields.
flashcards.example: ²³⁸U → ²³⁴Th + ⁴He. Smoke detectors use americium-241 alpha source.

flashcards.definition: Fast electron (n → p + e⁻). Moderate ionisation. Stopped by ~3 mm Al. Deflected opposite to α.
flashcards.example: ¹⁴C → ¹⁴N + e⁻. Used for thickness monitoring in paper mills.

flashcards.definition: EM wave, no mass/charge. Weakly ionising. Highly penetrating — reduced by thick lead/concrete. Not deflected.
flashcards.example: Cobalt-60 gamma source for cancer radiotherapy and equipment sterilisation.

flashcards.definition: Time for half the nuclei in a sample to decay. Constant for each isotope. After n half-lives: (½)ⁿ remains.
flashcards.example: I-131: t½=8 days. After 24 days (3 half-lives): ⅛ of original remains.

flashcards.definition: Determines age of organic material by measuring remaining ¹⁴C (t½=5730 y). Effective up to ~50,000 years.
flashcards.example: Dead tree with 25% original ¹⁴C: 2 half-lives → ~11,460 years old.

flashcards.definition: Heavy nucleus (U-235) splits after absorbing neutron → smaller nuclei + 2-3 neutrons + energy. Chain reaction.
flashcards.example: ²³⁵U + n → ¹⁴¹Ba + ⁹²Kr + 3n + energy. Used in nuclear reactors and bombs.

flashcards.definition: Two light nuclei combine into heavier nucleus + energy. Powers stars. Requires extreme T and P.
flashcards.example: ²H + ³H → ⁴He + n + 17.6 MeV. Clean energy source — experimental on Earth (ITER).

flashcards.definition: Fission neutrons cause more fissions → exponential growth. Controlled in reactors (control rods absorb excess neutrons).
flashcards.example: One U-235 fission → 3 neutrons → 3 more fissions → 9 neutrons → ... Controlled by boron control rods.

flashcards.definition: Radiation that can remove electrons from atoms → ions. Damages DNA → mutation/cancer risk.
flashcards.example: Alpha is most ionising (dangerous if ingested). Gamma penetrates deeply (dangerous externally).

flashcards.definition: Low-level radiation from natural and artificial sources: radon gas (~50%), cosmic rays, rocks, medical procedures.
flashcards.example: Average UK dose: ~2.7 mSv/year. Radon from granite bedrock is the largest natural contributor.

flashcards.definition: Boron or cadmium rods that absorb neutrons, controlling fission rate. Insert fully = shutdown.
flashcards.example: SCRAM: emergency shutdown — all control rods fully inserted, absorbing all neutrons.

questions.stem: Which radiation is stopped by paper?
questions.explanation: Alpha is a helium nucleus — large, highly ionising, stopped by a few cm of air or paper.

choices: Fast-moving electron emitted when neutron → proton
questions.explanation: Beta decay: n → p + e⁻ (+ antineutrino). Mass number unchanged; atomic number increases by 1.

questions.stem: Half-life of I-131 is 8 days. After 24 days, what fraction remains?
²³⁸₉₂U → ²³⁴₉₀Th + X. What is X?
questions.explanation: Mass drops by 4 (238→234), atomic number drops by 2 (92→90). This is alpha decay.

questions.stem: Why is alpha most dangerous if source is inside the body?
choices: Highly ionising — all energy absorbed over a very short distance in living tissue, causing concentrated damage
questions.explanation: Alpha particles deposit all their energy in a tiny volume → intense localised damage. Outside body, dead skin layer stops them.

questions.stem: Which is NOT deflected by electric/magnetic fields?
choices: Gamma — no charge, EM wave, travels straight
questions.explanation: Only charged particles are deflected. Gamma is electromagnetic → no charge → no deflection.

questions.stem: Fission chain reaction is controlled in a reactor by:
questions.explanation: Boron/cadmium control rods absorb neutrons, keeping the multiplication factor = 1. Fully inserted = shutdown.

questions.stem: Why is fusion difficult to achieve on Earth?
choices: Nuclei repel each other (positive charges) — extreme temperature (~100 million °C) needed to overcome Coulomb barrier
questions.explanation: Electrostatic repulsion between nuclei. Gravity in stars provides containment. On Earth: magnetic confinement (tokamaks) or lasers.

questions.stem: Technetium-99m (t½=6 h) is used as medical tracer because:
choices: Short half-life — decays quickly after imaging, minimising patient radiation dose. Gamma emitter detected externally
questions.explanation: Short t½ = patient not radioactive for long. Gamma penetrates body → detected by gamma camera. Ideal tracer properties.

questions.stem: A sample has count rate 1200 cpm. After 30 min, 150 cpm. Half-life?
Background radiation must be subtracted from experimental readings because:
choices: It's always present and would inflate the measured count — subtracting gives true count from the source
questions.explanation: Geiger counters detect background radiation even with no source. True count = measured − background.

choices: Fuel abundant (deuterium from seawater), no long-lived radioactive waste, no meltdown risk
questions.explanation: Deuterium from seawater essentially unlimited. Helium product is inert. Reaction self-limits if conditions fail — no runaway possible.

questions.stem: Gamma source kept in lead box. Why?
choices: Gamma is highly penetrating — lead provides shielding, absorbing radiation
questions.explanation: Dense materials like lead absorb gamma photons. Thickness required depends on gamma energy. Inverse square law also used (distance).

questions.stem: ¹⁴₆C → ? + e⁻. What is the daughter nucleus?
choices: ¹⁴₇N — beta decay: atomic number increases by 1
questions.explanation: Beta decay: n→p+e⁻. Mass stays 14, atomic number 6→7. Nitrogen-14.

choices: E=mc² — some mass is converted to energy when nucleus splits. Products have slightly less total mass than original
questions.explanation: The total mass of fission products + neutrons is slightly less than the original uranium + neutron mass. This 'missing mass' became energy: E=mc².
